creator.name: Protocol Minute

description: Short, source-pinned explainers of the protocols the web runs on. Every on-screen claim is checked against the RFC it comes from.
name: Protocol Minute
tagline: One protocol idea a minute, checked line by line against its RFC.

videos.description: Iris asks and Theo, who has read the source, explains how WebSockets work straight from RFC 6455: an ordinary HTTP request that upgrades to one two-way connection. They follow that connection from the Upgrade handshake and the Sec-WebSocket-Accept proof, through the frame header and client masking, to ping, pong and the closing handshake. Every factual line is checked against a pinned snapshot of RFC 6455.

card.note: RFC 6455 offers one TCP connection instead, carrying traffic in both directions.
card.sub: Before WebSockets, pages polled the server; RFC 6455 calls that an abuse of HTTP.
card.title: Cold open

card.note: If the server accepts, it answers 101 Switching Protocols with an accept header; any other status and HTTP semantics still apply. Then frames flow both ways.
card.sub: An ordinary HTTP request asks to upgrade: Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, a random key and protocol version 13.
card.title: The opening handshake

card.note: The accept value proves the server actually read a WebSocket handshake.
card.sub: The server appends a predefined GUID to the client's key, takes the SHA-1 hash of the result and base64-encodes those 20 bytes.
card.title: The accept key

card.note: Every client frame is masked: a 4-byte key XORed over the payload, so a script can't choose the bytes on the wire. Servers never mask theirs.
card.sub: Each frame starts with a FIN bit, then a 4-bit opcode: text, binary or a control frame. 7 bits of length cover up to 125 bytes; longer payloads use the next 2 or 8 bytes.
card.title: The frame

card.note: Either side sends a close frame, such as status 1000 for a normal closure; the other answers with its own close, and the server shuts the TCP connection.
card.sub: Send a ping and the other end must answer with a pong carrying the same data. Close, ping and pong are never fragmented and carry at most 125 bytes.
card.title: Control frames

card.note: Ask once in HTTP. Then talk in frames.
card.sub: A WebSocket is one HTTP request that turns into frames, both ways.
card.title: The whole board
